t: Sort Integers by The Power Value — Collatz Steps with Memoization
o: For each integer x in [lo, hi] we must compute its Collatz 'power' (steps to reach 1), then sort the range by (power, value) and return the k-th element. In Example 1, powers of 12..15 are [9,9,17,17], so the sorted order is [12,13,14,15] and k=2 gives 13. In Example 2, powers of 7..11 are [16,3,19,6,14], giving sorted order [8,10,11,7,9] and k=4 gives 7. Since hi <= 1000, there are at most 1000 numbers; the only real concern is computing each power efficiently. Intermediate values can exceed hi (e.g., odd steps triple values), so a memo table indexed by value should be sized generously or use a hash map.
k: The power function is deterministic and heavily overlapping: computing power(x) recursively reuses power(x/2) or power(3x+1), so memoization turns exponential recursion into near-linear work per query.
Intermediate values can far exceed hi (e.g., 27 jumps to 82), so cache by actual value — a hash map or a large fixed array both work given hi <= 1000.
Sorting by pair (power, value) handles ties automatically; no custom comparator logic beyond that is needed.

a.i: Simulate the Collatz process for every number from scratch, counting steps until reaching 1. With at most 1000 numbers and powers bounded well below a few hundred steps, this is fast enough for the given constraints without any caching.
s: Define getPower(x): loop while x != 1; if x is even halve it, else set x = 3x+1; count iterations.
Build a list of pairs (power(x), x) for all x in [lo, hi].
Sort the list lexicographically by (power, value).
Return the integer part of the (k-1)-th pair.
a.t: O(n log n + n * P) where n = hi - lo + 1 <= 1000 and P is the max power (~180 for values up to 1000); sorting dominates asymptotically but everything is tiny.
a.sp: O(n) for the list of pairs.

a.i: Many numbers share subproblems: e.g., power(12) needs power(6), which also serves power(24). Caching power(v) for every visited value v (including intermediates above hi) makes each computation essentially O(1) amortized after warm-up. A hash map keeps the cache simple regardless of how large intermediates get.
s: Create a memo map with base case memo[1] = 0.
Define recursive power(x): if x is memoized return it; otherwise compute 1 + power(next(x)) where next halves even x or applies 3x+1 to odd x, store in memo, and return.
Compute power for every x in [lo, hi], forming (power, x) pairs.
Sort pairs by (power, value) and return the (k-1)-th value.
a.t: O(n log n) overall — each distinct value's power is computed once in O(P) amortized (P ~ 180 max chain length), and sorting n pairs dominates.
a.sp: O(n + M) where M is the number of distinct cached values (intermediates included); bounded by a few thousand here.

w: In an interview, start with brute force simulation to show correctness, then add memoization as the optimization — it demonstrates recognition of overlapping subproblems (the DP/memoization tag). Pitfalls: forgetting that intermediate values exceed hi (so don't size a fixed cache by hi alone — use a hash map or a generously sized array like 1,000,000 entries); using int overflow is not an issue since 3x+1 stays well within 32-bit range for x <= 1000; remember tie-breaking by ascending value, which a pair sort handles naturally. Edge cases: lo == hi (answer is lo), k = 1 or k = hi - lo + 1. Likely follow-ups: what if hi were 10^6 or larger (precompute sieve-style DP over a fixed table), or can you find the answer without full sorting (quickselect on the pair key for O(n) average).
